title: Dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) for borderline
description: Dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) is a therapy designed for borderline personality disorder. Over many months it teaches skills for handling intense emotions, tolerating distress and getting on with other people. After DBT, the amygdala, which flags emotional events, responds less to upsetting pictures, and people report handling their emotions better. In the first part, brightness shows how the brain differed from people without the condition before treatment. In "What changed", brightness shows the change since before treatment: warmer means more than before, violet means less than before.
caveat: The main finding comes from one study of 11 people with borderline personality disorder and 11 without, before and after 12 months of DBT, and a review of the 9 studies that have looked at the brain after DBT. These are small studies, the review notes that research on this is still scarce, and the main study had no group of people with borderline personality disorder who did not have DBT, so changes over time cannot all be credited to DBT. Another study found that the drop in amygdala activity in response to pain was smaller after DBT, a different measure from the one drawn. The review names the anterior cingulate without saying which part; it is drawn on the dorsal part, which is an assumption. How the brain differed from people without the condition before treatment is not drawn, because the sources read report it only as background. These are averages across groups of people, not a picture of any one person's brain. Treatments help many people, not everyone, and in different ways. This is not medical advice: talk to a doctor or therapist about what is right for you.

phases.name: Before treatment
phases.caption: Before therapy. The comparison here starts from each person's own level, so the brain is drawn at rest.

phases.name: A year of DBT
phases.caption: Weekly individual therapy and skills groups; a year in the main study, 12 weeks of inpatient DBT in another. People were not scanned during this time.

citations.title: Dialectical behavior therapy alters emotion regulation and amygdala activity in patients with borderline personality disorder.
citations.quote: Event-related fMRI was obtained pre- and post-12-months of standard-DBT in unmedicated BPD patients.

phases.name: What changed
phases.caption: After DBT, the amygdala responds less to emotional pictures than before, most clearly on the left and to pictures seen a second time. A review of studies also describes less activity in the anterior cingulate. People who settled faster to repeated upsetting pictures reported handling their emotions better.

phases.name: What stayed the same
phases.caption: Only a few small studies have looked at the brain after DBT. The inferior frontal gyrus responded less to arousing pictures but more during tasks that need self-control, so it is not drawn as one change.

order.rationale: This last part is a summary of what the studies did not find or did not measure, not a later point in time.

regions.explanation: Less active after 12 months of DBT, compared with the change over the same time in people without the condition, in one study of 11 patients; the reduction was most marked on the left. A review of 9 studies also describes reduced amygdala activity after DBT, but its amygdala evidence is two studies, one of them this one.

The review does not say which part; it is drawn on the dorsal anterior cingulate, which is an assumption. One study also found that the link between the left amygdala and the dorsal anterior cingulate during pain changed after DBT, at trend level.

These effects were reduced after DBT, as compared with patients with treatment as usual.
